titolo: Desolvation‐Induced Network Reformation and Cracking in the Single Crystals of Hydrogen‐Bonded Frameworks Composed of Tetraazaanthraquinone and Anthraquinone Derivatives
abstract: AbstractA molecular‐level understanding of how structural transformations induce morphological changes in organic crystals is essential for developing flexible crystalline materials. Herein, we report that two solvated hydrogen‐bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) undergo structural transformations, giving rise to crystal crack propagation in the directions corresponding to their molecular displacements. The HOFs are composed of the tetracarboxylic acids, 4,4′,4″,4′″‐(5,10‐dioxo‐5,10‐dihydropyrazino[2,3‐g]quinoxaline‐2,3,7,8‐tetrayl)tetrabenzoic acid (TAAQ) and 4,4′,4″,4′″‐(9,10‐dioxo‐9,10‐dihydroanthracene‐2,3,6,7‐tetrayl)tetrabenzoic acid (AQ), incorporating tetraazaanthraquinone and anthraquinone cores, respectively. Although TAAQ and AQ have closely similar molecular geometries, their HOFs have entirely different hydrogen‐bonded networks. In both HOFs, we found that specific directional hydrogen bonds cleaved, and new hydrogen bonds re‐formed, resulting in quasi single‐crystal‐to‐single‐crystal transformations. The direction of molecular displacement and crystal cell shrinkage were aligned parallel to the crack propagation. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying micro–macro property correlations induced by hydrogen‐bond cleavage and re‐formation.Keywords: Crystal crack, Flexible porous material, Hydrogen‐bonded organic frameworks, Porous crystal, Structural transformation Two solvated hydrogen‐bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) based on tetraazaanthraquinone and anthraquinone were found to undergo quasi single‐crystal‐to‐single‐crystal transformations through hydrogen‐bond cleavage and re‐formation. These transformations induced crystal crack propagations, and molecular‐level correlations between the structural transformations and crack propagations were proposed for both HOFs.

sezioni.testo:
Flexibility of porous frameworks have gained widespread attention in the last two decades because of their high selectivity in separations, molecular recognition, and responsiveness to stimuli.[ 1 , 2 , 3 ] Hydrogen‐bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) are a class of attractive flexible frameworks,[ 4 ] which are formed by reversible hydrogen bonds (H bonds). Reversible H bonds allow HOFs to exhibit structural transformations via cleaving and re‐forming H bonds,[ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] in addition to other types of transformations such as breathing[ 9 ] and change of stacking manners.[ 10 ] H‐bond cleavage and re‐formation have the potential to bring remarkably dynamic properties and functionalities because networks and molecular arrays can change dramatically.
Transformation of H‐bonded networks can cause some changes in morphology of single crystals, such as deformations,[ 11 , 12 , 13 ] crack propagations,[ 14 ] and pulverizing.[ 15 ] The relationship between changes in network structures and crystal morphology needs to be clear for further understanding about dynamics of soft crystals.[ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] However, there have been limited reports on this topic in the field of HOFs, whereas their properties and functionalities arising from their transformations have been widely explored.[ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] As examples of network transformation that caused crystal cracks, we have reported a few HOFs composed of tetracarboxylic acids. [ 7 , 27 ]
To control the H‐bond cleavage and re‐formation is one of the challenges. Extending the comprehension of the relationship between network transformation and crystal cracks can lead to finding the key molecular structure for controlling network transformation. Through an in‐depth review of previously studied re‐formable HOFs, we noticed that the o‐bis(4‐carboxyphenyl)aryl (o‐CPA) moiety could play a key role in the H‐bond cleavage and re‐formation. To date, several to a dozen HOFs containing the o‐CPA moieties, including 4,4′‐dicarboxy‐o‐terphenyl (DoT) moiety, have been reported to exhibit H‐bond cleavage and re‐formation.[ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ]
Herein, we report H‐bonded network transformation and transformation‐induced crystal cracks observed in two novel HOFs TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1, which are composed of tetracarboxylic acids TAAQ and AQ possessing o‐CPA‐incorporated tetraazaanthraquinone and anthraquinone cores, respectively (Figure 1a). The molecular structures are quite similar to each other; only the imine nitrogen atoms at 1,4,5,8 positions in TAAQ were replaced by sp2‐carbon in AQ. However, TAAQ‐1 has the layered square lattice ( sql ) network formed by dimerization of carboxy groups, whereas AQ‐1 has a triangle motif with partial dimerization of carboxy groups (Figure 1b). Despite the differences in their H‐bonded network structures, both two HOFs showed structural transformations by cleaving and re‐forming H bonds. The structures before and after the transformations were successfully identified by single‐crystal X‐ray diffraction (SCXRD) analysis. Based on SCXRD analysis and theoretical calculation, we found that cleaved H abonds are a little weaker than the retained ones. Moreover, anisotropic cracking in the single crystals were observed during the transformation (Figure 1c). We revealed that the cracks propagated in the single crystals were parallel to the plane on which molecules were moved to be re‐formed. These results can contribute to molecule‐based reticular chemistry and to development of new flexible porous framework materials.

## Synthesis and Crystallization
TAAQ was synthesized by condensation of 1,2,4,5‐tetraaminobenzoquinone (1) with dimethyl 4,4′‐oxalyldibenzoate (2) followed by hydrolysis of resultant ester 3 (Schemes 1a and S1a). AQ was synthesized through a palladium catalyzed cross coupling between 2,3,6,7‐tetrabromoanthracene‐9,10‐dione (4)[ 28 , 29 ] and (4‐(methoxycarbonyl)phenyl)boronic acid (5), followed by hydrolysis of resultant ester 6 (Schemes 1b and S1b). TAAQ and AQ were characterized by 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy (Figures S23–S26) and HRMS.
To prepare crystalline HOFs, TAAQ was recrystallized from a mixed solution of N,N‐dimethylformamide (DMF) and 1,2,4‐trichlorobenzene (TCB) at 75 °C to yield solvated HOF TAAQ‐1 as dark yellow block crystals suitable for SCXRD analysis (Figures 2a and S1).[ 30 ] Recrystallization of AQ was attempted using various solvent systems. Light yellow block crystals (Figures 2b and S2a) or pale yellow plate crystals (Figure S2b) were obtained by recrystallization at 75 °C using a mixed solution of DMF and o‐dichlorobenzene (DCB). Pale yellow needle crystals (Figure S2c) were obtained from a mixed solution of DMF and TCB. These crystals were subjected to SCXRD analysis, indicating that they all had the same frameworks (AQ‐1), although the diffraction pattern sufficient for the analysis was obtained only from block crystals.
The transformed HOFs were prepared by heating the crystals of TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1 at 70 °C under reduced pressure, giving the second forms TAAQ‐2 and AQ‐2, respectively. These structures were also revealed by SCXRD analysis.
## Crystal Structure
Crystal structures of TAAQ‐1 and TAAQ‐2 are shown in Figures 3 and S4. Both belong to the space group P‐1. The unit cell of TAAQ‐1 contains one TAAQ molecule. TAAQ has an inversion center in the tetraazaanthraquinone core, and the core structure is almost flat (the root‐mean‐square deviation RMSD: 0.0679 Å). The twisted angles (ω) between the core and two independent phenylene groups are 19.5° and 62.5°. The peripheral carboxy groups of TAAQ form a dimer through the self‐complementary H bond with a O⋯O distance of 2.59–2.61 Å to give a sql topological 2D networked sheet (Figure 3a). The sheet contains rhombic voids with aperture dimension of 7.2 Å×15.0 Å. The sheets are stacked in an inclined AA pattern along the a axis with an interplanar distance of 3.61 Å (Figure 3b). Multiple interactions including CH⋯π, CH⋯N, and CH⋯O interactions along the a axis were observed between layers. TAAQ‐1 has inclusion channels with rectangular‐shaped apertures with 6.7 Å×11.0 Å (Figure 3c). The void ratio was estimated to be 37% by PLATON.[ 31 ] The guest molecules TCB were severely disordered, making it difficult to determine their alignments in TAAQ‐1.
TAAQ‐2 has cross‐shaped carboxylic acid tetramers by combination of the carboxylic acid dimer and other two carboxyl groups (Figures 3d). The tetramer is similar to those formed in other tetracarboxylic acid‐based HOFs after transformations.[ 5 , 7 , 8 ] The unit cell of TAAQ‐2 contains one TAAQ molecule, which has an inversion center in the core. The conformation of TAAQ molecules was little changed, including the flatness of the core with RMSD of 0.0486 Å and the twisted angles between the core and the phenylene groups (ω = 19.5° and 60.7°). In the cross‐shaped carboxylic acid tetramers, the O⋯O distance in the carboxylic acid dimer part is 2.69 Å and that of the branched H bonds is 2.81 Å, which is slightly longer than the former. The stacking manner along the a axis was almost retained, but the interlayer distance decreased into 3.49 Å (Figure 3e). TAAQ‐2 has the channels with narrow aperture with 2.1 Å × 6.6 Å (Figure 3f), and the void ratio was estimated to be 9%, indicating that the void shrank to one‐fifth of its initial size.
On the other hand, AQ constructed a completely different network from TAAQ‐1. AQ‐1 has trigonal channels, which were given by forming carboxylic acid dimers (Figure 4a). The unit cell of AQ‐1 contains three molecules (Z = 3), i, i’, and ii (shown in blue, light purple, and yellow, respectively, in Figure 4c). Molecule i’ is related to molecule i by the inversion symmetry operation. Molecule i has the curved anthraquinone core with RMSD of 0.165 Å (curvature: 14.7°) (Figure S5). Molecule ii has the almost flat core with RMSD of 0.0168 Å (curvature: 0°) and also has the inversion center in the core. The twisted angles between the core and each phenylene groups are 46.5°, 46.7°, 51.1°, and 54.1° in molecule i and 52.5° and 52.9° in molecule ii. These values are close to the angles in other HOFs composed of carbocyclic aromatic compounds such as benzene derivative[ 32 ] and naphthalene derivative.[ 8 ] All four peripheral carboxy groups of molecule ii form dimers through the self‐complementary H bond with a O⋯O distance of 2.56–2.63 Å. In contrast, two peripheral carboxy groups of molecule i form dimers with a O⋯O distance of 2.58–2.63 Å, whereas the other two of molecule i does not form dimers, which probably have H bonds with the solvent molecules DMF (Figures 4d and S6). Molecules of AQ were stacked through multiple interactions including π⋯π, CH⋯π, and CH⋯O interactions along the a axis, as shown in Figure 4b,e. AQ‐1 has inclusion channels with triangular‐shaped aperture with 6.7 Å × 5.7 Å (Figure 4f). The void ratio was estimated to be 31% by PLATON.[ 31 ] The interactions among guest molecules DCB and the oxygen atoms of anthraquinone core were observed (Figure S6a,b).
AQ‐2 has ladder H‐bonded networks, where the H bonds of carboxylic acids trimer were found (Figure 5a). The unit cell of AQ‐2 also contains three molecules i, i’, and ii (Figure 5c). The conformation of AQ molecules were little changed, including the curvature of the core (14.9° in molecule i, 0° in molecule ii) (Figure S5) and the twisted angles between the core and each phenylene groups (ω = 45.0°, 50.4°, 51.0°, and 56.7° in molecules i and ω = 43.1° and 55.2° molecule ii). In the trimer, the O⋯O distance of carboxylic acids dimer is 2.56–2.72 Å and that of the branched H bonds are 2.82 Å. In addition, H bond was observed with a O⋯O distance of 2.72 Å between the oxygen atom of the anthraquinone core and the carboxylic acid (Figure 5d). The stacking manner along the a axis was almost retained (Figure 5b,e). The channel along the a axis seen in AQ‐1 completely disappeared. The internal space is fully occupied by inclusive guest molecules (Figure 5f), which were aligned by the interaction with the oxygen atom of the anthraquinone core.
## Effects of Core Composition in Molecular Stacking
What is the effect of incorporating imine nitrogen atoms into the anthraquinone core? We noticed that each molecular stacking manner of TAAQ and AQ in their HOFs were significantly different. Moreover, their stacking manners were almost retained during H‐bonded network transformations. To explore the origin of the difference, we focused on electrostatic potential mappings and the intermolecular interaction energies between stacked molecules.
TAAQ and AQ exhibit the different electrostatic potential distributions (Figures 6a, S14, and S15). In the molecule TAAQ, the center of tetraazaanthraquinone core is highly positively charged, whereas the oxygen and nitrogen atoms of the core are negatively charged. In TAAQ‐1, TAAQ stacked in layers without rotation, shifting along the a axis shown as Figure 6b. Molecules of TAAQ were aligned in such a way that the positively charged center of the core overlaps with the negatively charged edges of the core. On the other hand, in the molecule AQ, the center of anthraquinone core has positive charge, but not as high as that in TAAQ. The negative charged edges of the core were also found in AQ, although it was not as widespread as in TAAQ.
Based on the expectation that the interactions between the cores of the stacked molecules result in the different stacking manners of TAAQ and AQ, we calculated the interaction energies between stacked molecules (E mol ), in addition to those between stacked cores (E core ), as listed in Table 1 (Figures S16–S18). The calculated interaction energies revealed that the interactions between the cores make a minor contribution to the total interactions of stacked molecules in both TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1.
Then, we focused on the stacking interactions involving the peripheral phenylene groups. In TAAQ‐1, the interaction was found between the hydrogen atom of the upright phenylene group (ω = 62.5°) and the quinone oxygen atom (the CH⋯O distance of 2.62 Å). This hydrogen atom of the phenylene group also contacts the nitrogen atom of the core (the CH⋯N distance of 2.75 Å). Another notable interaction is π⋯π interaction between the pyrazine ring and the phenylene group (ω = 19.5°). The distance of their centroids in the rings is 3.71 Å and the dihedral angle of the rings is 19.5°. In AQ‐1, the interaction was found between the hydrogen atom of the upright phenylene group (ω = 46.5° and 54.1° in molecule i and ω = 52.5° in molecule ii) and the quinone oxygen atom (the CH⋯O distance of 2.36 Å and 2.52 Å), as shown in Figure 6c. Their distances are shorter than those in TAAQ‐1, indicating that these interactions contribute to the unique stacking manner in AQ‐1. The π⋯π interaction was found between the phenylene groups in the molecule i and ii (ω = 51.1° in molecule i and ω = 52.9° in molecule ii). The distance of their centroids in the rings is 3.89 Å and the dihedral angle of the rings is 10.0°. This arrangement is similar to the ideal slipped‐parallel benzene dimer,[ 33 ] indicating that this π⋯π interaction can also make a significant contribution to the stacking manner in AQ‐1.
On the basis of these considerations, it can be concluded that the composition at 1,4,5,8‐positions of the core modulated the conformation of the peripheral phenylene rings, giving the different molecular interactions. The sp2‐carbon atoms in AQ give the upright phenylene groups, which favor both the CH⋯O and π⋯π interactions. These interactions lead to the formation of the rotated stacking structure.
## Removal of Guest Molecules
To investigate the release behavior of guest molecules, the thermogravimetric (TG) and differential thermal (DT) analyses were conducted. The bulk crystals of TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1 obtained from mixed solutions of DMF and TCB were analyzed for comparison. We noted that AQ‐1 can be obtained using either DCB or TCB as guest molecules, although the structure shown in Figure 4 was of the DCB solvate. TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1 showed total weight loss of 53% and 59%, which corresponds to a host–guest ratio of 1:4 and 1:6, respectively (Figures 7 and S27). The TG curve of TAAQ‐1 indicated that TCB are released in two steps. Three‐fourths of TCB molecules are released in the first step up to 156 °C. The other TCB molecules are released in the second step up to 297 °C. In contrast, the TG curve of AQ‐1 has no clear plateau under 210 °C, suggesting continuous release of the guest molecules. TCB began to desorb gradually at room temperature and completed desorption at 210 °C. In both AQ‐1 and TAAQ‐1, additional heating beyond 350 °C resulted in weight loss, corresponding to the onset of decomposition. According to the differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1 exhibited five and three endothermic events, respectively (Figure S11). A combined analysis of the TG curves and the DSC profiles suggests that each step of guest release contains two endothermic events.
To investigate their transition behaviors triggered by removal of guest molecules, variable‐temperature powder X‐ray diffraction (VT‐PXRD) patterns were recorded on as‐formed bulk crystals of the solvated HOFs as heated from room temperature to 355 °C (Figures S9 and S10). Although the simulated and experimental patterns did not show good agreement, no other polymorphic structures were identified through a series of SCXRD measurements performed on multiple crystals. VT‐PXRD patterns indicated that TAAQ‐1 exhibited two‐step transformations, occurring at approximately 125 and 215 °C. According to the TG analysis, the guest molecules were completely removed in the phase obtained after heating to 297 °C, which is referred to as TAAQ‐3. The PXRD pattern corresponding to TAAQ‐3 indicated that it retained periodicity to some degree. AQ‐1 exhibited a transformation at 85 °C, and then, its structure was maintained up to 355 °C. The porosity was examined by gas adsorption experiments only for TAAQ‐3 (Figures S12 and S13) as AQ‐2 does not possess any 1D channel in its crystal structure. The adsorption isotherms of TAAQ‐3 indicated no significant micropore adsorption, which means that TAAQ‐3 possesses little or no porosity.
## H‐Bonded Network Cleavage/Re‐Formation and Crystal Morphology Changes
We revealed that both AQ‐1 and TAAQ‐1 can change their H‐bonded network, although their H‐bonded networks were totally different. Interestingly, cracks propagated along a specific direction in the crystals of both two HOFs during removal of guest molecules. To elucidate the mechanism about how the molecules were rearranged, we discuss the correlations between H‐bond cleavage/re‐formation and the crystal crack propagation.
Following the logic described in our previous study,[ 7 ] we compared intralayer and interlayer rearrangements as follows. To form a new H bond with the donor oxygen atom A (shown in blue sphere in Figure 8a), there are two candidate receptor oxygen atoms B1 and B2 (shown in red and purple spheres, respectively). When the A and B1 form a new H bond during the transformation, i.e., intralayer molecular rearrangement occurs, the distance between A and B1 is 9.66 Å. When the A and B2 form a new H bond during the transformation, i.e., interlayer molecular rearrangement occurs, the distance between A and B2 is 9.06 Å. This means that A is closer to B2 than B1, indicating that interlayer rearrangement is more likely to have occurred. In Figure 8b, the cell diagram as viewed from the (001) plane of TAAQ‐1 is compared with the corresponding one of TAAQ‐2. This diagram visually illustrates the close proximity of A and B2.
Moreover, cracks emerged parallel to the (120) plane in the crystal of HOF TAAQ‐1 (Figures 8d,e, and S3). In the (120) plane, A and B2 are aligned (Figure 8b), supporting our speculation. Figure 8c shows the cell shrinkage as viewed along the [120] direction. The cell has shrunk parallel to the (120) plane and along to the c axis, coinciding with the direction of molecular displacement during the transformation. In contrast, only slight shrinkage was observed along the [120] direction. This result reinforces the logic that we previously proposed, in which crystalline domains parallel to the crack propagation are retained.
These insights about H‐bond re‐formation, cell shrinkage, and crack propagation were further applied to AQ‐1. Again, AQ‐1 and AQ‐2 have similar yet unique molecular conformations and stacking manners. Assuming that these molecular conformations and stacking manner are almost retained during the transformation, the proposed molecular rearrangement mechanism is illustrated in Figure 9a. In this mechanism, the molecules are displaced parallel to the (100) plane, approximately along the [011¯] direction. The oxygen atoms, colored green, pink, and orange, represent H‐bonding sites that form new H bonds after the transformation.
Cracks propagated parallel to the (100) plane in both the platelet and block crystals of AQ‐1 (Figures 9c,d, and S3). On the plane parallel to (100), each pair of oxygen atoms marked with the same color (green, pink, and orange in Figure 9a) is aligned, supporting the proposed mechanism of molecular displacement parallel to the (100) plane. Figure 9b shows the cell shrinkage as viewed along the [100] direction. The cell has shrunk parallel to the (100) plane and along the [011¯] direction, coinciding with the direction of molecular displacement during the transformation. In contrast, only slight shrinkage was observed along the [100] direction.
To provide a quantitative analysis, the interaction energies of H bonding were calculated (Tables S2, S3, and S18–S27; Figures S7, S8, S19, and S20). The calculated energies suggested that the H bonds perpendicular to the direction of molecular displacements are strongest in both TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1. In TAAQ‐1, H bonds are formed along two directions, [11¯0] and [011¯], highlighted in light blue and orange, respectively, in Figure 8a. The corresponding intermolecular interaction energies are −128 and −119 kJmol−1, respectively. Stronger H bonds were retained and weaker ones were cleaved, in good agreement with our proposed molecular rearrangement mechanism. In AQ‐1, H bonds are formed along three directions: [011], the b axis, and the c axis. The corresponding intermolecular interaction energies are −91, −133, and −102 kJmol−1. Along the direction [011], two H bonds with an energy of −91 kJmol−1 run parallel in close distance. Although these H bonds are weaker than the others, this molecular arrangement contributes to the structural stability along the [011] direction. We also confirmed interaction anisotropy and network robustness visualized as the energy frameworks using CrystalExplorer[ 34 ] (Figures S21 and S22). These depictions further support our speculation of H‐bond network cleavage and re‐formation.

In this study, we have deciphered crystal cracks caused by cleaving and re‐forming H bonds in solvated HOFs. HOFs TAAQ‐1 and AQ‐1 have rhombic and trigonal networks, respectively. During removal of guest molecules, the specific directional H bonds were cleaved and re‐formed, whereas the others were retained. Based on the crystal structures and detailed observation of the crystals, we revealed that the crystal cracks propagated parallel to the direction of cell shrinkages and perpendicular to retained H bonds of carboxylic acid dimers. According to calculated interaction energies, the retained H bonds are stronger than the cleaved ones. We demonstrated the relationship among H‐bonded network transformations, unit cell shrinkages, and crystal cracking in several types of H‐bonded networks, not limited to sql networks.
